clue.text: Dance at H.Q.? What a game !

parts.note: headquarters is an operating base
a ball is a formal dance

explanation.surface: Someone marvels at a dance being held at headquarters.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in clue order: a ball held at base. The exclamation 'What a game!' is the definition, an American sport.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a bat-and-ball sport, the national pastime of the United States.

clue.text: Money, in the North, that is in a club

parts.note: brass is northern English slang for money
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: Someone up north keeps their cash in a club.
explanation.walkthrough: The club is a golf club: an old wooden-headed club roughly equal to a two-wood, so named for its brass sole plate.
explanation.definitionFit: An old golf club, a wooden-headed driver with a brass sole.

clue.text: It's of little significance, figuratively speaking

definitions.text: It's of little significance, figuratively speaking

parts.words: It's of little significance, figuratively speaking
parts.note: reads as something unimportant, but describes a small figure: a little sculpture is literally a figure, and small

explanation.surface: A dismissive remark that something hardly matters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figuratively speaking' seems to soften the remark, but it says the thing is a figure, and 'little' says it is a small one.
explanation.definitionFit: A small carved or cast figure is a little piece of sculpture.

clue.text: Is it analogous to a cake of soap ?

definitions.text: Is it analogous to a cake of soap ?

parts.words: Is it analogous to a cake of soap ?
parts.note: a bar of soap is used in the tub; the clue asks for a cake whose name puts it in the tub too

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about something resembling a bar of soap.
explanation.walkthrough: A cake of soap belongs in the bath; this sweet bun is named after the spa town of Bath, a city in the west of England, so it sounds like a bathroom cake.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet yeast bun topped with sugar, named after the English spa city.

clue.text: Cat'I let out of the window

indicators.note: letting something out frees it from its arrangement, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone lets a cat out of the window.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges the seven letters of CAT I LET. 'Let out of the window' reads as freeing the cat, but the window is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A lattice window has small panes set in a crisscross of lead strips.

clue.text: Sounding like Runyon's Harry, with a sore throat

indicators.note: a word that sounds like another is spoken the same, so this signals a homophone

parts.note: Harry the Horse is a gangster in Damon Runyon's Broadway stories

explanation.surface: A gravelly voice is compared to a Runyon gangster's.
explanation.walkthrough: Damon Runyon was an American writer of Broadway tales; one of his characters is Harry the Horse, and his nickname sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough, croaky voice is what someone with throat trouble has.

clue.text: One doesn't step on it to remain stationary

definitions.text: One doesn't step on it to remain stationary

parts.words: One doesn't step on it to remain stationary
parts.note: a car's foot brake is stepped on; this other parking brake is pulled by hand to keep the vehicle still

explanation.surface: Advice on keeping a car still without pressing a pedal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Step on it' also means drive fast, the opposite of staying still; the real point is that this brake is worked by the hand, not the foot.
explanation.definitionFit: The parking brake of a car is a lever pulled by the driver's hand.

clue.text: Such is the reasoning of a churchman in first-class surroundings

indicators.note: surroundings go around something, so the first-class letters are placed outside the churchman

parts.note: A1 means first-class, written AI
a prior is the head of a priory, a churchman

explanation.surface: A clergyman reasons from his comfortable first-class quarters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in ... surroundings' puts PRIOR inside AI (A1, first-class). The Latin phrase names reasoning from first principles rather than experience.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase describes deduction made before, and independent of, observed evidence.

clue.text: Persevering, Crockett's minister ?

definitions.meaning: to ... is to persevere, to keep going
S. R. Crockett wrote The ... Minister, about a Scottish minister who failed to gain a parish; ... is Scots for failed

explanation.definitionFit: Read as two words it is keeping at a task; as one Scots word it is the failed minister of S. R. Crockett's book.

clue.text: Adjustment — make it to a panda

indicators.note: to make something of these words is to form a new word from their letters

explanation.surface: Someone asks for an adjustment to turn something into a panda.
explanation.definitionFit: An adaptation is a change made to suit new conditions, an alteration.

clue.text: This drama no doubt had a drop scene

definitions.text: This drama no doubt had a drop scene

parts.words: This drama no doubt had a drop scene
parts.note: a drop scene is a painted stage curtain; the clue pretends it means a scene full of drops, as from the sky

explanation.surface: A theatre note about a play's painted curtain.
explanation.walkthrough: The play is Rain, the stage version of Somerset Maugham's story; a drop scene is a theatre drop curtain, here taken as raindrops.
explanation.definitionFit: Rain is the name of a famous play from Maugham's story, and also falls in drops.

clue.text: One thing the tripper doesn't miss, apparently

definitions.text: One thing the tripper doesn't miss, apparently

parts.words: One thing the tripper doesn't miss, apparently
parts.note: a tripper sounds like a holidaymaker, but here is someone who trips; what they fail to miss is the obstacle that trips them

explanation.surface: A remark about a sightseer who never misses an attraction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tripper' looks like a day-tripper; read it as one who trips, and what such a person never misses is the thing they stumble over.
explanation.definitionFit: An obstacle or hindrance, literally something that trips a walker.

clue.text: Understanding-—of the terms of the Common Market ?

definitions.text: Understanding-—of the terms of the Common Market

parts.words: Understanding-—of the terms of the Common Market
parts.note: an understanding between nations, a French word, as used in the language of the European Common Market

explanation.surface: A question about grasping the conditions of the Common Market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Understanding of the terms' reads as comprehension, but the clue wants a friendly agreement between states, a French term of the sort the Common Market (the European Economic Community) used.
explanation.definitionFit: A friendly agreement between nations, from the French word for understanding.

clue.text: Mongol warrior took a less exciting way

parts.note: tamer means duller, less exciting
a lane is a way or narrow road

explanation.surface: A Mongol fighter chooses a duller route.
explanation.definitionFit: Timur, the fourteenth-century conqueror of Central Asia, is known in English by this name.

clue.text: The show to watch for a change

definitions.meaning: a ... show is a stage entertainment of mixed acts
doing something for ... means doing it for a change

explanation.definitionFit: It is a music-hall entertainment of mixed turns, and a change from the usual.

clue.text: How to get out of a Crete taxi ?

definitions.text: How to get out of a Crete taxi ?

indicators.note: getting out of something takes these letters out of their order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A tourist asks how to escape from a Cretan cab.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get out of' rearranges CRETE TAXI, and the whole clue also describes the answer: freeing yourself from the cab.
explanation.definitionFit: To free oneself or someone from a tight place.

clue.text: The little beast we blame for disorder

indicators.note: the letters are put into disorder, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone blames a small creature for the mess.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for disorder' rearranges WE BLAME.
explanation.definitionFit: A young female sheep is a small farm animal.

clue.text: Carousal as the cutter turns to leave harbour

indicators.note: something that turns round faces the other way, so the cutter is read backwards

parts.note: a saw is a cutting tool
to sail is to set off from port

explanation.surface: A party starts as a cutter swings round to put to sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turns' reverses SAW, the cutter, to give WAS. A cutter looks like a boat, which fits the harbour; here it is a tool.
explanation.definitionFit: Wassail is a drinking bout or festive revelry, as well as a toast.

clue.text: Country of drinkers ?

parts.note: animals that drink by lapping could be said to live in a land named for them

explanation.surface: A question about a nation fond of drink.
explanation.walkthrough: To lap is to drink like a cat or dog, so the northern region of Scandinavia is read as a land of lappers.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arctic region of northern Scandinavia, home of the Sami people.

clue.text: Spanish translation of "Hard Cash "?

parts.note: looks like the title of a book (Charles Reade's novel Hard Cash) in Spanish, but means the coins Spain used

explanation.surface: A note on a Spanish edition of a novel called Hard Cash.
explanation.walkthrough: Hard Cash is a Victorian novel by Charles Reade, so the clue seems to ask for a book title; it wants Spanish coins, which are literally hard cash.
explanation.definitionFit: These were the coins of Spain before the euro, real money in Spanish.

clue.text: It was true in the case of Annie Laurie

definitions.text: It was true in the case of Annie Laurie

parts.words: It was true in the case of Annie Laurie
parts.note: in the Scottish song Annie Laurie, 'Annie Laurie gave me her' pledge 'true'

explanation.surface: Something was true when it came to Annie Laurie.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scottish song Annie Laurie has the line 'And 'twas there that Annie Laurie gave me her promise true', so the missing word completes the lyric.
explanation.definitionFit: An undertaking or vow given to someone, which the song's heroine kept faithfully.

clue.text: One thing one can always measure up to

definitions.text: One thing one can always measure up to

parts.words: One thing one can always measure up to
parts.note: to measure up to something is to equal it; everyone is exactly as tall as their own height

explanation.surface: A reassuring remark about a standard nobody fails.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Measure up to' means reach a standard; read literally, you always measure up to your own height.
explanation.definitionFit: Height is the measure of a person's body standing upright.

clue.text: They're not prosecuted for uttering false notes

definitions.text: They're not prosecuted for uttering false notes

parts.words: They're not prosecuted for uttering false notes
parts.note: uttering a forged banknote is a crime; voicing a wrong musical note is not

explanation.surface: Counterfeiters escape charges for passing forged banknotes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Uttering' is the legal word for passing forged money, and 'notes' look like banknotes; here they are musical notes sung off key.
explanation.definitionFit: Vocal performers may hit a wrong note without breaking any law.

clue.text: Religious over-work

parts.note: the theological term for good works done beyond what God requires

explanation.surface: A complaint about doing too much for the church.
explanation.walkthrough: In Catholic theology this is the performance of good works beyond those required for salvation, literally paying out more than is asked.
explanation.definitionFit: The theological doctrine of works done beyond what duty demands.

clue.text: She can only dance with a band

annotationWithheld.why: She can only dance with a band (4): no parse found giving TARA; the clue reads as a cryptic definition but which sense of 'dance with a band' points to the name is unclear
annotationWithheld.clue: She can only dance with a band

clue.text: Reassemble a skeleton, so to speak

definitions.meaning: to ... bones is to join them at the joints, as when mounting a skeleton

explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to connect by joints, and also to pronounce words clearly.

clue.text: Led Peg to make a solemn promise

indicators.note: the letters are used to make something new, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone escorts Peg to the altar to take a vow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to make' rearranges LED PEG.
explanation.definitionFit: A binding vow or undertaking given formally.

clue.text: They're young and hare-brained

parts.note: hare-brained means foolish, but here these young animals really do have the brains of hares

explanation.surface: A grumble about foolish youngsters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hare-brained' means reckless; taken literally, young hares have hare brains.
explanation.definitionFit: Young hares in their first year are known by this name.
